title: Token throttle crossover lab notes
content:
Objective:
Quick scratchpad to track experiments that try to reproduce intermittent 401 vs 429 behavior when clients rotate API keys or rapidly request ephemeral tokens. Keep steps, raw command outputs, timestamps and short hypotheses in one place so I can hand off to SRE or paste into a postmortem later.

Summary of what we've seen (high-level):
- Clients report bursts of 429s that correlate with ephemeral key creation spikes.
- In many reproductions we see a few 401s mixed in; 401 often precedes a cluster of 429s by ~3–6s.
- Pattern is stronger for short-lived keys (TTL < 60s) and for clients that re-use the same key header across multiple concurrent requests.

Hypotheses (short):
1) Token registration race: new key not yet propagated to auth cache; first request returns 401 -> client retries quickly -> hits quota window limit or throttling -> 429.
2) Global rate-window accounting: creating keys increments some global counter for a window and momentarily reduces allowed throughput per-key; simultaneous creations push overall request rate beyond the newly tightened per-key budget.
3) Proxy/caching TTL mismatch: edge cache has stale deny/allow mapping for a key for a short period which leads to early 401s; backend then enforces rate limits generating 429s.
4) Client-side retry confusion: client sees 401, rotates key and retries N times immediately; rotation + immediate retries cause spike and trigger 429s.

Experiment log (step-by-step):
(Use these reproducible commands locally against staging-redwood.)

Environment: staging-redwood, region=us-west-2, routing-policy=prefer-local, default client concurrency=12.

Experiment A: single new ephemeral key, sequential requests-
- create key: curl -sS -X POST https://stg.api.redwood.ai/v1/keys -H 'Authorization: Bearer admin-token' -d '{"ttl":60}' | jq -r '.token'  # saved as K1
- single request: curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer K1" https://stg.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"hi","max_tokens":5}'
Result: 200 OK. No 401/429 in 1k sequential runs.

Experiment B: concurrent hammering immediately after issuance-
- spawn 40 concurrent curl requests using K2 (new key).
- bash snippet: for i in {1..40}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer $K2" https://stg.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate & done; wait
Observed output sample (timestamps):
  2026-01-12T15:12:05Z 200
  2026-01-12T15:12:05Z 401
  2026-01-12T15:12:06Z 429
  2026-01-12T15:12:06Z 429
  2026-01-12T15:12:06Z 200
Notes: Not deterministic but ~12–18% of runs include at least one 401 and 20–35% include >=1 429.

Experiment C: rotation pattern (simulate client that rotates on 401)
- flow: issue K3 -> start 20 requests -> if any 401 seen, create K4 and retry remaining batch with K4 immediately.
- pseudocode: see attached gist (TODO: add link).
Observed:
- 401 appears on 1–2 requests in batch -> client rotates -> immediate spike of retries -> 429 storm follows, lasting ~10–12s until throttle window slides.
- When we add exponential backoff (100ms -> 400ms) before retrying after 401, 429 frequency drops by ~70%.

Experiment D: artificially slow propagation (inject header to simulate delayed auth cache)
- toggled feature flag stg-auth/allow-cached=false to force fresh validation on each request (local flag): effect was fewer 401s but slightly more 429s.
Interpretation: suggests cache reduces window of 401s but can hide early throttles.

Raw error snippets collected:
- HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
  {"error":"invalid_api_key","message":"Key not found"}
- HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
  {"error":"rate_limit_exceeded","message":"per-key window exceeded: 60 req/60s"}
- full header capture: X-RateLimit-Limit: 60, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0, X-RateLimit-Reset: 1670000005

Metrics traces (notes):
- Correlate spikes in token creation (metric: tokens.created) with short dips in X-RateLimit-Remaining for keys created in the same 10s window.
- Trace suggests a central accounting job increments counter on creation and applies a soft limit for first 30s for new keys. Need teams to confirm.

Quick debugging commands used during triage:
- list recent tokens: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer admin-token' https://stg.api.redwood.ai/v1/admin/tokens?limit=50 | jq '.'
- capture headers: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" https://stg.../generate
- reproduce with python async clients (to simulate many concurrent requests properly): see snippet below:
  import asyncio, aiohttp
  async def r(k):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s:
      async with s.post(url, headers={'Authorization':f'Bearer {k}'}, json={'prompt':'x','max_tokens':10}) as r:
        print(r.status)
  loop = asyncio.get_event_loop(); loop.run_until_complete(asyncio.gather(*[r(K) for _ in range(40)]))

Things to check with SRE / Auth team:
- Is there any per-key "warmup" quota applied when keys are created? (I think so based on metric deltas.)
- Is key propagation to edge caches synchronous? If it is eventually consistent, what are typical propagation windows per region?
- Are creations/rotations counted against a global per-customer quota immediately? Could that momentary consumption reduce per-key capacity?

Immediate mitigation ideas for clients (short-term):
- Add a small jittered delay (50–250 ms) before the first burst after key creation.
- If client receives 401, do not rotate immediately; instead: wait 200–500ms and retry once — reduces cascade.
- Use exponential backoff on 429s and avoid immediate massive retries.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Add a deterministic repro harness (python asyncio) to repo: /tmp/token-throttle-repro (priority: high).
- [ ] Ask auth team: dump of key propagation logs for a 10s window after creation for a sample token id. (JIRA-INVEST-892 created.)
- [ ] Instrument edge cache to emit a trace when it first sees a new key id.
- [ ] Compare behavior between short TTL keys (<=60s) and longer ones (>=3600s).
- [ ] Run a canary with client-side jitter/backoff for 24h to measure reduction in 429s.

Notes to self (forgotten things):
- When running local hammer tests, ensure to set HTTP/1.1 keepalive off for some runs; connection reuse can mask behavior.
- Watch for clock skew between client and server: 401s could be issued for signed tokens if TTL windows are mis-calculated.

Reference snippets (for postmortem):
- "Client rotated key on 401 and issued 40 retries within <200ms causing global throttle window to be exceeded and 429 cascade."
- "Mitigations: client jitter and backoff; server: re-evaluate immediate counting on token creation and consider soft-enforcement windows that start after a short grace period (e.g., 250ms)."

End of scratchpad. Will refine and export final repro harness once core auth answers are in.
